content: Saul dressed David with his clothing. He put a helmet of bronze on his head, and he clad him with a coat of mail. {{v:39}} David strapped his sword on his clothing and he tried to move, for he had not tested it. David said to Saul, “I can’t go with these, for I have not tested them.” Then David took them off. {{v:40}} He took his staff in his hand, and chose for himself five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag which he had. His sling was in his hand; and he came near to the Philistine. {{v:41}} The Philistine walked and came near to David; and the man who bore the shield went before him. {{v:42}} When the Philistine looked around and saw David, he disdained him; for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and had a good looking face. {{v:43}} The Philistine said to David, “Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?” The Philistine cursed David by his gods. {{v:44}} The Philistine said to David, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and to the animals of the field.” {{v:45}} Then David said to the Philistine, “You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of the LORD of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. {{v:46}} Today, the LORD will deliver you into my hand. I will strike you and take your head from off you. I will give the dead bodies of the army of the Philistines today to the birds of the sky and to the wild animals of the earth, that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel, {{v:47}} and that all this assembly may know that the LORD doesn’t save with sword and spear; for the battle is the LORD’s, and he will give you into our hand.” {{v:48}} When the Philistine arose, and walked and came near to meet David, David hurried and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine. {{v:49}} David put his hand in his bag, took a stone and slung it, and struck the Philistine in his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the earth. {{v:50}} So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine and killed him; but there was no sword in David’s hand. {{v:51}} Then David ran, stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it out of its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled. {{v:52}} The men of Israel and of Judah arose and shouted, and pursued the Philistines as far as Gai and to the gates of Ekron. The wounded of the Philistines fell down by the way to Shaaraim, even to Gath and to Ekron. {{v:53}} The children of Israel returned from chasing after the Philistines, and they plundered their camp. {{v:54}} David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put his armor in his tent. {{v:55}} When Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the captain of the army, “Abner, whose son is this youth?” Abner said, “As your soul lives, O king, I can’t tell.” {{v:56}} The king said, “Inquire whose son the young man is!” {{v:57}} As David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand. {{v:58}} Saul said to him, “Whose son are you, you young man?” David answered, “I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite.”

facets.text: David refuses Saul's armor because he has not tested it, and goes out instead with a shepherd's staff, sling, and five smooth stones. The rejection of royal armor signals that David's victory will not rest on human military strength but on the LORD who has already delivered him from lion and bear. The scene teaches that God works through humble, tested means rather than the borrowed strength of the world.
facets.question: Why did David refuse to wear Saul's armor before facing Goliath?

facets.text: David frames the entire duel as a contest not between two warriors but between the gods invoked over each. Goliath curses David by his gods and boasts of sword, spear, and javelin, while David comes 'in the name of the LORD of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.' The confrontation reveals that Israel's true adversary is the blasphemer who has defied the living God, and that the outcome is a vindication of God's honor.
facets.question: What was the real conflict between David and Goliath about?

facets.text: David declares that the LORD 'doesn't save with sword and spear; for the battle is the LORD's,' locating the source of victory entirely in God. The purpose is explicitly evangelical: 'that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.' This anticipates the biblical pattern by which God delivers through weakness so that salvation is manifestly his work and not human achievement.
facets.question: What does it mean that the battle belongs to the Lord?

facets.text: David's triumph as the unlikely, unarmored shepherd who strikes down the towering enemy prefigures Christ, the true Son of David, who conquers the powers of evil not by force but through apparent weakness. The lone deliverer who fights for the whole people, wins by God's power, and beheads the enemy foreshadows the victory over sin, death, and the devil accomplished at the Cross. The shepherd-king points to the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the flock.
facets.question: How does David's victory over Goliath prefigure Christ?

facets.text: David strikes Goliath in the forehead and afterward takes the giant's own sword to cut off his head, and the enemy is destroyed by his own weapon. The tradition reads this as an image of how the powers of death are undone by their own instrument, echoing the crushing of the serpent's head promised in Genesis and fulfilled when Christ conquers death by dying. The champion's fall on his face and beheading mark a complete and public overthrow of the adversary.
facets.question: What is the significance of Goliath being killed by his own sword and struck in the head?

facets.text: Goliath disdains David because he is 'but a youth, and ruddy, and had a good looking face,' judging by outward appearance and physical might. His contempt embodies the worldly assumption that God's cause depends on visible power, an assumption the narrative overturns. The passage teaches that God does not see as man sees and often chooses the despised to shame the strong.
facets.question: Why did Goliath despise David, and what does it reveal about worldly judgment?

facets.text: The narrative closes with Saul repeatedly asking whose son this young man is, and David answering that he is 'the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite.' The emphasis on David's Bethlehem lineage quietly points forward to the Davidic covenant and to the Messiah who would be born of David's line in Bethlehem. The question of the youth's identity opens the larger question of Israel's coming king.
facets.question: Why does the account emphasize that David is the son of Jesse of Bethlehem?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: David defeats the Philistine Goliath by refusing human armor and trusting in the LORD of Armies, winning a victory that vindicates God's honor and prefigures Christ's triumph over evil; the episode closes by highlighting David's Bethlehem lineage.

[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: David rejects Saul's untested armor and takes only staff, sling, and stones, teaching that victory rests on God rather than borrowed worldly strength.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The duel is a contest between the blasphemer's gods and the living God; Israel's true enemy is the one who defied the LORD, and the battle vindicates God's honor.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: David proclaims the LORD does not save with sword and spear because the battle is the LORD's, so that all the earth may know there is a God in Israel.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The unarmored shepherd-deliverer who conquers through weakness prefigures Christ the Son of David defeating sin, death, and the devil at the Cross.
[TYPOLOGICAL | inferential]: Goliath struck in the head and beheaded by his own sword images the crushing of the serpent's head and death undone by its own instrument.
[MORAL | inferential]: Goliath's contempt for the ruddy youth reflects worldly judgment by appearance, which God overturns by choosing the despised to shame the strong.
[SCRIPTURAL | traditional]: The closing question about the son of Jesse the Bethlehemite points toward the Davidic covenant and the Messiah born in Bethlehem.
